highlights: # In Other News: Anthropic Breach Dispute, UEFI Flaw Hits Most Servers, Cloudflare AI Data Leak. Only machines that use network boot are exposed, and the flaw, found by Anthropic and Google researchers, became public months ahead of a planned January disclosure after AMI published a code fix, leaving organizations to seek firmware updates from their vendors. Cathedral, a cybersecurity startup founded by former DOGE staffers, says its AI agents found ways into Anthropic’s internal systems in less than 12 hours by abusing weaknesses in third-party business software, reaching meeting transcripts, salary and job offer data, and Slack discussions about the company’s most advanced models, according to a draft report reviewed by the Washington Post (paywalled). Anthropic, which received the findings through its bug bounty program, says only a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems was reached, that it cut off the startup’s access the same day, and that Claude conversations, source code and model weights were not affected.

highlights: Within days of its release, several of the company's key partners, including Microsoft, Google and Amazon, reported quarterly results that added fuel to existing market jitters around the artificial intelligence buildout. "Everybody's still full steam ahead on AI, but all the things around it took an interesting turn this week," Daniel Newman, CEO at Futurum Group, told CNBC in an interview on Friday. In its prospectus on Monday, the AI company disclosed a net loss for the first half of the year of $80 billion, alongside hundreds of billions of dollars' worth of compute commitments and more than 90 pages of risk factors. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX, but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible. And Oracle, one of the biggest spenders on AI data centers, said at its investor day on Wednesday that it will limit additional fundraising in the coming years to $20 billion, and will turn cash flow positive in the second half of next fiscal year.

highlights: # Google’s satellite AI server transmits its first response to Earth. The Project Suncatcher satellite generated a haiku about being in space. Google’s AI chip-equipped satellite has generated its first response from space. In a blog post on Friday, Google says it successfully booted up the satellite’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), allowing the on-board Gemma 4 model to follow through on a prompt to create a haiku about being in space:. The test is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, an experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers in space. Google launched the satellite into orbit earlier this month. “Next, we will continue with a series of tests to evaluate how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit,” Google says. “Verifying our TPUs can reliably execute workloads in space paves the way for our next milestone of twin interconnected satellites in 2027.”. * Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk.

latest.title: AI Is Destroying Academic Publishing - The Atlantic
latest.summary: # AI Is Destroying Academic Publishing. As a journal editor, I can say: The currency of academic social capital is collapsing. Weak scholarship was once easy to spot at a glance: The signs included ba...
highlights: # AI Is Destroying Academic Publishing. As a journal editor, I can say: The currency of academic social capital is collapsing. Weak scholarship was once easy to spot at a glance: The signs included bad writing, a lack of relevant citations, and little engagement with previous scholarship, such as a paper that promised a “novel” conceptual framework without acknowledging the many other papers making similar claims. As an associate editor of a bioethics journal, I’d make a quick “desk reject” decision and not send these articles for peer review, which effectively killed any hope of publication. Now I can say: AI is affecting every part of academic publishing. There are sentences that have all of the trappings of real arguments, but that rarely make sense—such as “Algorithmic triage functions less as a clinical tool than as an infrastructure of deferred accountability.” There are citations that refer only to open-access or highly cited articles, because the most popular LLMs can’t readily access paywalled journal articles, so they rely on what’s either free or described at length elsewhere.

Foundational AI startups raised, in a single quarter, double the whole of 2025 for that category, according to Crunchbase News. Travel tech raised $2.2 billion over three quarters, down from $3.7 billion a year earlier. One sector is accelerating on huge checks while the other is contracting on small ones. [...] The AI share of Series B keeps climbing. With about two-thirds already going to AI-focused startups, non-AI travel companies will struggle to close growth rounds without a clear AI case.
Strategic investors fill more of the gap. Booking Holdings’ planned $100 million Vayo investment is the template. Expect more incumbents to write checks or buy startups outright.

highlights: OpenAI is saying it has no plans to go public this year – but senior Wall Street executives say they fully expect it will happen in the first quarter of 2027, On The Money has learned. The artificial intelligence giant run by Sam Altman has been quick to shoot down rumors that it’s preparing to IPO imminently now that archrival Anthropic has filed its S-1 as a precursor to a deal that’s expected in late November. Altman has been among the AI industry’s top alarmists – as has Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei – although that isn’t stopping the latter from cashing in on an initial public offering that could value the company as high as $2 trillion, possibly even surpassing SpaceX’s record-breaking IPO. Meanwhile, finance bigs are warning Altman that his iPO window could be closing with rising fears of an AI bubble and competition for investor capital – not just from the Anthropic sale but also a planned massive secondary stock sale by Meta, as first reported by On The Money.

Only machines that use network boot are exposed, and the flaw, found by Anthropic and Google researchers, became public months ahead of a planned January disclosure after AMI published a code fix, leaving organizations to seek firmware updates from their vendors. Cathedral, a cybersecurity startup founded by former DOGE staffers, says its AI agents found ways into Anthropic’s internal systems in less than 12 hours by abusing weaknesses in third-party business software, reaching meeting transcripts, salary and job offer data, and Slack discussions about the company’s most advanced models, according to a draft report reviewed by the Washington Post (paywalled). Anthropic, which received the findings through its bug bounty program, says only a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems was reached, that it cut off the startup’s access the same day, and that Claude conversations, source code and model weights were not affected.

"Everybody's still full steam ahead on AI, but all the things around it took an interesting turn this week," Daniel Newman, CEO at Futurum Group, told CNBC in an interview on Friday. In its prospectus on Monday, the AI company disclosed a net loss for the first half of the year of $80 billion, alongside hundreds of billions of dollars' worth of compute commitments and more than 90 pages of risk factors. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX, but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible. And Oracle, one of the biggest spenders on AI data centers, said at its investor day on Wednesday that it will limit additional fundraising in the coming years to $20 billion, and will turn cash flow positive in the second half of next fiscal year.
